common_name: Mons. Jules Elie Peony (Early Silvery-Pink Double Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Mons. Jules Elie is one of the earliest peonies to bloom each spring.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake or ring the stems before the huge, heavy blooms open. Introduced in France in 1888, Mons. Jules Elie is prized for opening its enormous, silvery lilac-pink double blooms among the very first peonies of the season, giving it a head start on the rest of the border. The bomb-form flowers carry a light, pleasant fragrance and hold up reasonably well as cut flowers, though their sheer size and weight benefit from support in windy or rainy conditions. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may take a year or two to resume full bloom after transplanting.

common_name: Kelway's Glorious Peony (Large Fragrant White Double Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Kelway's Glorious was introduced by the famed English Kelway's nursery in 1909.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and stake the strong stems before the massive blooms open. Kelway's Glorious carries huge, rounded, pure white double flowers with a strong, sweet fragrance long considered among the finest of any peony, opening from blush-tinted buds to flowers that can reach 8 inches or more across on a vigorous, floriferous plant. It has remained a benchmark white peony among collectors and breeders for well over a century since its introduction by England's famed Kelway's nursery. Divide congested clumps only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may sulk for a year or two after transplanting.

common_name: Edulis Superba Peony (Early Fragrant Rose-Pink Double Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; dating to 1824, Edulis Superba is one of the oldest peony cultivars still widely grown.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Dating to 1824 and still in commerce two centuries later, Edulis Superba is one of the oldest peony cultivars widely grown today, opening rose-pink double blooms with a sweet, old-fashioned fragrance early in the peony season, often in time for Memorial Day in much of its range, which made it a traditional favorite for cutting for that occasion. Its long garden history is a testament to reliable vigor and dependable bloom rather than novelty, and established clumps can persist and flower for generations with minimal care. Divide only when necessary, since peonies resent disturbance and may take a year or two to resume full bloom after transplanting.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Perle d'Azur is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. Perle d'Azur, introduced from France in 1885, bears an extraordinary abundance of sky-blue, four-petaled flowers over a long summer season, covering the vine so thoroughly that established plants can look like a solid sheet of blue. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so it can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter, a far simpler pruning routine than the large-flowered old-wood types. Its vigor and free-flowering habit make it an excellent choice for scrambling through a large shrub or covering a fence quickly.

common_name: Etoile Violette Clematis (Deep Violet-Purple Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Etoile Violette is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. Etoile Violette produces a profusion of small, deep violet-purple flowers with contrasting yellow-cream stamens over a long midsummer season, on a vigorous vine well suited to scrambling through roses or large shrubs where it adds a long-lasting second wave of color. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter, avoiding the guesswork of pruning old-wood types. Its abundant, small-scale flowers and easy care have made it a favorite among gardeners looking for a low-maintenance, high-performing clematis.
